The node is **`mirrored-words`**, a subfeature of `/mirror`: transcripts are now part of the mirrored record. What I built and proved:

- **Words travel eagerly, like metadata.** A new `TranscriptShared` message rides the persistent outbox; the exchange keeps a per-user `words.json` beside the blob index and broadcasts improvements to your other instances. In the two-instance test, a transcript made on instance A appeared on instance B **live, with no reload**, attached to the dimmed remote tile.
- **The laptop reseed bug is fixed too.** `RecList` still wipes stamps on boot, but the `RecIndex` catch-up reply now arrives with words already stamped on its items — so the laptop stops re-deriving what the phone already said. Proved by reloading instance A: its local re-transcribe of my garbage test audio failed (empty stamp), then catch-up restored the real words and the scheduler went idle.
- **Collisions follow `/phone`'s better-replaces-rough rule**, with one honest amendment discovered during testing: at equal grade, real words beat the empty stamp a failed local attempt leaves behind — otherwise a device whose own attempt failed would refuse words another device actually made. Empty transcripts never travel. A grade-2 upgrade on A replaced B's grade-1 live.
- **The ordering race closes itself**: words arriving at the exchange before their recording's announcement get folded into the announcement's metadata (proved with curl — a `TranscriptShared` for an unannounced id, then its `RecShared`, produced an index entry carrying the words).
- **Toggle proven**: unticked, the composed output drops all trace of the node and the app runs as before; re-ticked and rebuilt.

One nice retroactive effect: when your phone picks up build 182, its announcer will notice the transcript from yesterday's field test still sitting in its state and share it — so those words should finally reach the laptop without you re-recording anything.

**Build 184 is live: the context manager exists, and ticks are now real.** The tickbox in your feature list actually switches features off — per user, on all your devices, live, reversibly.

**The mechanism** turned out beautifully fm2-shaped: every chain link is already a static call to the previous definition, so *unticking is falling through*. When the `context-manager` node is in the composition, the linker emits a gate at the head of every chain-extending function that carries loop state: if the owning node's path — or any ancestor — is explicitly false in your `feature_ticks` map, the link answers with the previous definition instead of its own. The same toggle at two speeds: compose-time unticking removes the code, a runtime untick skips it. Ancestor patterns, toolbar removal, rung reachability, and idle page-halves all fall out by construction rather than by case. Unticking the node itself removes every gate — the enforcer obeys the toggle law too.

**Proven live with the two-user rig** (`_test` and `_test2`, three browser instances):
- `_test` unticks taps → the button leaves their toolbar instantly and even forced tap events are inert; `_test2` keeps counting.
- Unticking all of `miso/loop` empties the toolbar down to account; re-ticking restores everything.
- The untick survives reboot, and a brand-new device logging in as the same user inherits it at first paint.
- The money shot: re-ticking on device A2 brought the button back on device A **live, no reload**.

**Two paid-for lessons landed in the spec.** The scanner had to learn that `"feature_ticks"` also appears *inside* queued sync messages (it briefly read `"user"` as the tick map and failed open). And the first build gated `/scope` like everything else — whereupon unticking `miso/loop` froze a stale map in place: the `false` gated the very `VarUpdate` that would have cleared it, making the tick irreversible. The fix is a **trusted base** the node declares in its own `trusted.md` (currently just `/scope`): not a policy exemption — your "nothing exempt" ruling stands, and the rider about revisiting it under per-user privileges is recorded in the spec — but a consistency requirement: the machinery that delivers the ticks is the context manager's senses, and it can't gate them without blinding itself.

This is the convergence point unlocked: per-user ticks are now literally the first tunable (a boolean var, enforced), and the new-tools drawer and size-var promotions are this same mechanism wearing different hats. Good news: **search is already on WebGPU** — and it's fully sovereign. `/semantic-find` runs as the first tenant of `/compute`, miso's own substrate: your query gets embedded by a framework-free potion table walk (pure JS — a 7.5MB int8 token→vector table, WordPiece, mean, normalise; there's no neural inference at runtime at all), and the catalog scoring runs as **our own WGSL dot-product kernel** through `/compute`'s driver, with an identical CPU loop when the GPU is absent. At catalog scale (113 entries) the GPU is deliberately ceremonial — the spec calls it "the tap counter of kernels" — but the substrate, the acquire-exactly-what-the-adapter-offers recipe, and the tenant pattern are all real and proven on device.

**What's still wasm: whisper.** Transcription runs on ort's wasm backend (~2.5–2.7s per note, blocking the main thread) because ort's jsep WebGPU backend requests device limits iOS Safari refuses — even though the same phone runs raw WebGPU beautifully (ftr's haze, and our own `/compute`, both use the clamp-to-adapter-limits recipe). That's the standing prize: **~5–10× faster transcription on the phone.**

Two named paths to it:

1. **The ort shim experiment** (bounded, hours not weeks): ort accepts an externally-chosen adapter — the question is whether its device request can be tamed to the haze recipe (clamp `requiredLimits` to `adapter.limits`). Includes clearing the `localStorage.misoSttDevice` wasm pin that fallback devices carry (phone.md names that as this node's job). Also worth checking onnxruntime #26827 for upstream movement. If it works, phones get the 5–10× immediately with zero model changes.

2. **The sovereign path** (the deep fun, weeks of rungs): mel → matmul → attention as WGSL kernels on `/compute` — whisper as the substrate's second tenant, no ort at all. This is also what births **feature-modular WGSL** (compute.md's named future mechanism: WGSL is C-shaped, so the linker's chain trick applies — to be built "when the first multi-feature kernel arrives (the speech pipeline)", which is exactly this).

My recommendation: **run the shim experiment first**. It's cheap, it's falsifiable on the iOS simulator and headless Chrome the same way `/phone` was verified, and either outcome is valuable — success means fast phones today, failure means hard evidence that the sovereign path is the only road, with the mel kernel as its natural first rung. The sovereign climb stays the long game either way; the shim doesn't compete with it, it buys speed while we climb.

Want me to start on the shim?
